coverage.note: Corrections come from the full audit of 2026-09-26: two independent readers per lesson, a third settling disagreements, reconciled with the 2026-09-24 hand sweep (a hand check of 20 scored rows found 17 right). 839 fixes the tutor voiced or typed, filed in an approved rule, are counted. Uses are machine-counted: every time his Arabic exercises the rule, right or wrong; a fix with no counted use within 2 s counts as a use too, so a rule never has more mistakes than uses. Unscored = no counter sees his right uses of the rule, so its fixes are listed but no % is given. Asks: his own questions about a form (rule M1). Untested = he never used it in any recorded lesson, or it is a sound (F). Not taught yet = the tutor has not taught the rule (her notes, 2026-09-27): no score, left out of every total. 17 corrections are shown but not counted (the tutor's notes: not taught yet, or not a mistake - list in data/amal-grammar-notes-2026-09-29.json). A score built from a lesson that is not verified yet is marked with ≈ (hover or tap it for why).

audit.method: Amal re-says one of Medi's words in another shape (voice within 25s, or typed in the Meet chat), or names the rule in English. Words are compared across Arabic script, Latin and Arabizi. Scored against a hand-labelled gold set (docs/data/grammar-goldset.json). Never guessed: UNFILED when no rule fits.

rules.name: el- (the)
rules.one_line: `el-` marks a thing you already know; nothing marks a new one.
rules.why: English has 'a' and 'the'. Arabic only has 'the' - leaving it off is how you say 'a'.
more: "el" is used for general nouns: el-tuffaa7 zaaki = apples are delicious; el-shita baared = winter is cold. (Tutor)
Sun and moon letters: no need. Not a priority - do NOT mark it as an error if he doesn't use them correctly. (Tutor)
So a sun/moon-letter slip (el-shams vs esh-shams) is never scored. Only el- there / not there counts.

rules.name: idafa (possession)
rules.one_line: Thing first, owner second - and the first word never takes `el-`.
rules.why: There is no word for 'of'. You just put the two nouns next to each other.
more: el-bait Medi is always wrong - the first noun drops el-.
The LAST noun decides whether the whole phrase is definite.
bait m3allem = a teacher's house.  bait el-m3allem = the teacher's house.
If a noun ends with a possessive pronoun it's definite and doesn't take "el": bait u5ti = my sister's house; bent u5t jaarti = my neighbor's niece. (Tutor)

rules.name: possessive endings
rules.one_line: Stick the owner on the end of the word.
rules.why: Instead of 'my name', Arabic says 'name-my' as one word.
more: The set: -i my, -ak your (m), -ek your (f), -o his, -ha her, -na our, -kom your (pl), -hom their.
baiti my house, baitha her house, baithom their house.
Biddi and 3indi conjugate with possessive endings (they are not real verbs): biddo = he wants, 3indna = we have. (Tutor)
After a vowel: -ak -> -k, -ek -> -ki, -o -> long vowel + h: kursik = your (m) chair, awa3iki = your (f) clothes, abuh = his father. (Tutor)
Possessive endings also give object pronouns on verbs, except "me" is -ni: a3tini = give me, a3tih = give him. (Tutor)
Dual -ain words: eed -> eedayy, eedaik, eedaiki, eedaikom, eedaih, eedaiha, eedaina, eedaihom. (Tutor)
ijer -> ijrayy, ijraik, ijraiki, ijraikom, ijraih, ijraiha, ijraihom, ijraina. (Tutor)
daan/denain -> dinayy, dinaik, dinaiki, dinaikom, dinaih, dinaiha, dinahom, dinaina. (Tutor)
7awalain -> 7awalayy, 7awalaik, 7awalaiki, 7awalaikom, 7awalaih, 7awalaiha, 7awalaihom, 7awalaina. (Tutor)
Not every dual works like this (no "youmayy"); the list grows as he learns more. (Tutor)

rules.name: gender on adjectives
rules.one_line: Feminine noun takes a feminine adjective.
rules.why: Adjectives change shape to match the noun - usually by adding -a or -e.

rules.name: plurals
rules.one_line: Some add an ending, many change shape, and two has its own form.
rules.why: Arabic has three plurals: regular endings, irregular reshapes, and a special 'exactly two'.
more: Regular: -een (people, m) and -aat (things/f) - muwazzaf -> muwazzafeen.
Irregular: you memorise them - bait->byoot, bab->bwaab, shubbak->shababeek.
Exactly two: add -ein - yom->yomein, saa3a->saa3tain.

rules.name: kaan + verb = used to / was doing
rules.one_line: kaan + a present verb: something you used to do, or were doing (past continuous).
rules.why: kaan plus a present verb puts it in the past: over and over back then, or going on at that moment.
more: Also means past continuous: kunet aqra2 = I was reading; kaanat tetbu5 = she was cooking. (Tutor)
The b- after kaan: some verbs keep it, some drop it. It is NOT a rule - b- kept or dropped after kaan is never marked wrong. (Tutor)
kaan bishrab ahwe kul yom he used to drink coffee every day.
kaan laazem goes with this too: kaan laazem + past = should have; kaan laazem + present = should have OR had to. The tutor advises using it with the present. Scored under B16. (Tutor)
Taught in lessons: the tutor corrected this 1 time(s) out loud (09-24 sweep). No longer a gap rule - scored (Medi 2026-09-25).

rules.name: bakoon / ykoon
rules.one_line: No 'to be' in the plain present - but bikoon comes in for habits, for biddi/3indi in the past and future, and to mean 'probably'.
rules.why: This is the 'being' verb that appears only in certain slots.
more: Plain now: drop it - ana ta3baan.
Habitual with usually / sometimes / every: 3aadatan bikoon mash8ool 3ala el-wa7de = he's usually busy at 1:00. (Tutor)
With biddi / 3indi in the past and future it is REQUIRED: kaan biddi = I wanted; ra7 ykoon 3indi = He will have. (Tutor)
With lamma / iza: lamma ykoon biddak = when you want; iza bikoon 3indak = if you have. Here it is NOT strict - leaving it out after lamma / iza is not marked wrong. (Tutor)
Bikoon can also mean "probably": bikoon m3asseb halla = he's probably angry now; bitkoon teshte8el = she's probably working. (Tutor; her Doc's autocorrect wrote "Bitcoin teshte8el")
To check with the tutor: she glossed ra7 ykoon 3indi as "He will have"; ykoon 3indi reads as "I will have".

rules.name: make-X vs get-X
rules.one_line: Doubling the middle letter turns 'I become' into 'I make someone'.
rules.why: One is about you, the other is about what you do to somebody else.
more: bad7ak I laugh -> bada77ek I make people laugh.
baz3al I get sad -> baza33el I make someone sad.
bazha2 I get bored -> bazahhe2 I bore people.
7 pairs in her Doc, plus ba3asseb.
rules.tally_title: Make-X vs get-X verb pairs: babse6 / banbese6, baz3ej / banze3ej

rules.name: verb matches its subject
rules.one_line: The verb's person, gender and number must match who or what is doing it.
examples: the company that sells it washes it (sharika is feminine -> bet-)
what excites you? (one thing -> singular verb)
rules.why: English verbs barely change ('I/you/they sell'). Arabic verbs change for every person: a feminine noun takes the she-form, a plural takes -u, 'I' takes a-/ba-.
more: Present tense: the prefix/ending must be the right person - bey3asseb-ni (it annoys me), not ba3asseb-ni; testa3mel (she uses), not testa3meli.
A noun subject decides the form: the cup enkasarat (feminine), meetings bey-zah2u-ni (plural).
Past-tense endings for ana/inta/hiyye stay in B5; adjectives stay in A8.

rules.name: words that drag a ma along
rules.one_line: `abadan` is not enough on its own - the verb still needs `ma`. And after `abel` it is always `abel ma` + a bare present verb.
rules.why: Two different -ma's that pull opposite ways on the b-.
more: abadan ma baru7 - keeps the b-, because abadan is real negation.
After abel it's always ma + the present verb with no b-, even when the English is past: abel ma aaji = before I came. (Tutor)
abel ma yiju (before they come) - that -ma is part of the conjunction, not negation.
ba3ed-ma teshra7i (after you explain) - same, and the b- drops.
Other words / prepositions take ma as well; the tutor will explain them later. (Tutor)

candidates.why: abadan needs ma on the verb; she prompted 'أبدًا شو؟' and he said ما يجي.

rules.name: iza / lamma
rules.one_line: if, when - conditional words. lamma drops the b- on the next verb, iza keeps it.
rules.why: lamma drops the b- (B3); iza keeps it. Both bring in bikoon before an adjective or biddi / 3indi (B8).
more: lamma = when (it will happen).  iza = if (it might).
These are conditional words: they need bikoon before the adjective, or before biddi and 3indi, in their sentence. (Tutor)
lamma drops the present marker b-; iza does not. (Tutor) lamma aru7 when I go - bare verb.
Iza (if) KEEPS the b (Tutor): iza bteji, never iza teji.
Scoring: under B8 the tutor wrote that bikoon after lamma / iza is not strict, so leaving it out is not counted (asked Medi 2026-09-30, since this note says 'require').

candidates.why: iza keeps the b-; Amal supplied بنروح and he repeated it.

rules.name: illi
rules.one_line: 'the one that' - never changes shape. No el-, no illi.
examples: the thing I like the most
there is a song that I know
rules.why: One word covers that / which / who, for everything - but only after a definite word.
more: No el, no illi: if the word before illi is not definite (no el- and no possessive ending), don't add illi. (Tutor)
aktar ishi ba7ebbo = the thing I like the most; seyyarti illi basoo2ha = my car that I drive; fi u8niyye ba3rafha = there is a song that I know. (Tutor)
It never changes for gender or number.
The clause after it usually needs the C2 pointer ending - ishtareto not ishtarait.

rules.name: question words
rules.one_line: The basic set.
rules.why: Arabic doesn't need a 'do' helper - the question word just goes first.
more: shu what, wein where, keef how, 2adaish how much, kam how many, lesh why, meen who, aymta when.
Addaish and kam both mean how much / how many; they're used differently and build the sentence differently. (Tutor)
kam always takes the singular: kam dars = how many lessons. (Tutor) See E5.
kam also means few: 3indi kam ishi = I have a few things. (Tutor)

rules.name: word order
rules.one_line: Normal is verb then object; front the object and C2 kicks in.

rules.name: preposition goes in front
rules.one_line: English leaves it dangling; Arabic never does.
examples: where did you buy it from?
rules.why: The preposition fuses to the question word and leads the sentence.
more: min wein from where, lawein to where, 3an shu about what.
ma3 meen with who, min emta since when, min shu from what.

rules.name: noun, not verb, after a preposition
rules.one_line: After bi / fi / min use the noun of the action, not a verb.
examples: I'm known for cooking kebab (bi + el-tabe5, not bi + a6bo5)
rules.why: English uses '-ing' after 'for/at'. Arabic uses the action's noun: tabe5 = cooking.
more: Amal 09-21 38:15: 'the noun. Noun is طبخ' (her chat: ana ma3roof bi el-tabe5 el-kabab).
Proposed by the 09-24 sweep (NEW-C11); approved by Medi 2026-10-02 (GR-18). Which preposition a word takes stays in D2.

rules.name: prepositions
rules.one_line: Small words with several jobs each.
rules.why: Each one covers 2-4 English prepositions, so you learn them by use, not translation.
more: min from, 3ala on/about, fi in, ma3 with, bi by/with, la to/for.
3ala alone covers on, about, against and owing.

rules.name: verb + its fixed preposition
rules.one_line: The verb chooses it. You can't guess from English.
rules.why: Learn the verb and its preposition as one unit.
more: ba6lub min - ask FROM (not 'to').
5aayef min - scared FROM (not 'of').
mishtaa2 la missing TO, 2al2aan 3ala worried ON, mu5talef 3an different FROM.

rules.name: preposition keeps el-
rules.one_line: Where English drops 'the', Levantine keeps it.
rules.why: English says 'from home' and 'by car' with no 'the'. Arabic puts it back.
more: bi / la / fi fuse with it: bi-l..., la-l..., fi-l...
min / 3ala / ma3 keep it separate: min el-bait, 3ala el-6aawle.
No el- on a name (la-Mehdi, fi America), on something already owned (ma3i, ma3 sadiqi), or when it really is indefinite (ma3 3aseer).

rules.name: endings on prepositions
rules.one_line: Stick the person on the end of the preposition. All take endings except bi.
rules.why: Same idea as A4, but on prepositions instead of nouns.
more: All prepositions take endings except "bi". (Tutor)
ma3i with me, ma3ak with you, ma3o with him.
minni from me, minnak from you, minno from him.
Some double their letter: min -> minno, not mino.
la- has its own endings: ili, ilak, ilek, ilkom, ilo, ilha, ilhom, ilna. (Tutor)
fi is like the others with small changes: fiyy, fik, fiki, fikom, fiyyo, fiha, fihom, fina. (Tutor)

rules.name: iyyaa - the second object
rules.one_line: A verb carries only one pronoun; a second one rides on `iyyaa`.
rules.why: You cannot stack two object endings on one verb, so the second gets its own word.

jeeb-li = bring me. jeeb-li iyyaa = bring it to me.

rules.name: number + noun
rules.one_line: 2 has its own form; 3-10 take a plural; 11+ take a SINGULAR.
rules.why: The rule flips twice as the number gets bigger - this is the part English never prepares you for.
more: Exactly 2: no number word, just the -ein ending - yomein, saa3tain.
3 to 10: the number without its -e / -a ending + the plural noun: 5ames da2aaye2 = 5 minutes. (Tutor)
talat iyyaam, 5ams saa3aat.
11 and up: number + SINGULAR noun - 7da3sh yom, 3ishreen saa3a.
Taught in lessons: the tutor corrected this 3 time(s) out loud (09-24 sweep). No longer a gap rule - scored (Medi 2026-09-25).

rules.name: kam + singular
rules.one_line: After `kam` (how many) the noun is always singular - never plural.
rules.why: English asks 'how many' with a plural noun. Levantine keeps the noun singular after kam, even though the answer is many.

rules.name: vowel length
rules.one_line: Holding a vowel longer changes the word.

rules.name: mufaddal + 3ind
rules.one_line: Mufaddal (favorite) is an adjective that follows its noun and matches it in gender and definiteness; a noun with a pronoun ending counts as definite, so it takes el-mufaddal, and 3ind + the person can support it when it stands alone or after the noun.
examples: this is his favorite ice cream
rules.why: English puts 'favorite' before the noun and never changes it, but in Arabic mufaddal comes after the noun and has to agree with it, and 3ind makes it a matter of preference.
more: Formula: noun-ending + el-mufaddal/e/a/een; el-mufaddal + 3ind + person

rules.name: kamaan: also vs another
rules.one_line: Kamaan meaning 'also / too / as well' can go anywhere in the sentence, but kamaan meaning 'another / one more' goes before the noun.
examples: Heyye kamaan bet7eb el-baid / heyye bet7eb el-baid / kamaan heyye bet7eb el-baid
She also likes eggs. (example by Claude, spelling unverified)
Another / one more thing. (example by Claude, spelling unverified)
This is my fiancée's favorite dish too.
هذي الأكلة المفضلة عند خطيبتي كمان.
This dish is my fiancée's favorite too. (example by Claude, spelling unverified)
rules.why: English uses two different words, 'also' and 'another', while Arabic uses kamaan for both, so only its place in the sentence shows which one is meant.

rules.name: taani and 8eir
rules.one_line: taani before a noun means second; after the noun without el- it means another; 8eir before a noun means a different or other one, and 8eir + 3an means different from.
rules.why: English uses different words for second, another and different, but Arabic uses the same words, so the meaning depends on word order and context.
more: Formula: taani + noun = second | el- + noun + el-taani = the second / the other | noun + taani = another | 8eir + noun = different / other

The tutor wrote it: «taani and 8eir 
Taani has two particularly useful functions: identifying something as second in a sequence and referring to something additional or different.
Rule 1: Taani + noun = Second / the second…
When taani comes before a noun, it can identify the second item or stage in a sequence.
Structure: taani + noun
Meaning: Second / the second…
Rule 2: El- + noun + el-taani / el-taaniye = The second» - her example: taani 7ada = second person / the second person yoami el-tani = my second day, 8eir bluze = another/different shirt, ishi taani = something else, huwwe 8eir 3anni = he is different than me. (Tutor)

rules.name: awal / aa5er with el-
rules.one_line: Awal and aa5er + a noun without el- mean first / last, but with el- or a possessive ending they mean the beginning / end of, so to say 'first' or 'last' there, use illi or put the adjective after the noun (el-awal / el-oola, el-a5eer).
rules.why: English uses 'first' and 'last' the same way everywhere, but in Arabic el- or a possessive ending on the noun turns them into 'the beginning of' and 'the end of', because idafa overrules the other rules.

rules.name: hidden gender nouns
rules.one_line: Some nouns have a gender that does not match how they sound: they sound masculine but are feminine, or sound feminine but are masculine. This is not only for nature words (sun, fire, earth, sky, air) but also for words like hand, leg, eye, ear, girl, man and war.
examples: So when does the sun rise? (example by Claude, spelling unverified)
The fire burned me. (example by Claude, spelling unverified)
Fire burns. (example by Claude, spelling unverified)
The sun bothers me. (example by Claude, spelling unverified)
rules.why: The gender of these nouns does not match their sound, so a learner cannot guess it from the word's shape and has to learn each one.
more: Formula: sound ≠ gender: شمس shams = feminine; نار nar = feminine; أرض ard = feminine; سما sama = feminine; حرب 7arb = feminine (sounds masculine); هواء hawa = masculine
Claude heard the tutor teach it in the 2026-10-08 lesson at 37:46: «يعني it's feminine but it sounds masculine or it's masculine» (AM-32)
Close to A8 gender on adjectives: A8 says a feminine noun takes a feminine adjective, but it assumes you already know which nouns are feminine; this rule covers nouns whose gender is hidden.
Added by the tutor on the Tutor page 2026-10-17 (AM-31). No automatic detection yet: counted only from the readers and the tutor's and the student's notes until a person adds a detector.
